# Incident Report — DESKTOP-ES9F3ML Malware Infection

**Evidence reviewed:** `2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (51,181 packets, 26.4 MB, ~624s capture; packet timestamps 2026-01-28 03:04:03–03:14:27 UTC). No IDS/Suricata alert exports or other artifacts were present in the evidence directory — this pcap is the sole source for every finding below.

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.1.21.58** | Source of all infection traffic |
| MAC address | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** | DHCP Discover/Request frames, ARP |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** | DHCP `Host Name` option; mDNS/NBNS; matches Kerberos SPN `host/desktop-es9f3ml.win11office.com` |
| AD domain | WIN11OFFICE.COM (DC: WIN-LU4L24X3UB7, 10.1.21.2) | Kerberos realm, LDAP/CLDAP SRV queries |
| Logged-in user | **gwyatt** | Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REQ, `CNameString=gwyatt`, requesting service tickets for `krbtgt/WIN11OFFICE.COM` and `host/desktop-es9f3ml.win11office.com` at t=20.2s |
| LAN gateway / DHCP server | 10.1.21.1 (MAC 00:04:c1:be:8c:d4), domain `mshome.net` | DHCP ACK |

## 2. Malware Family

**Behavioral classification: commodity information-stealer with an integrated browser-fingerprint/anti-fraud evasion module, consistent with the "Lumma Stealer"-class malware-as-a-service delivered through a fake-download / ClickFix-style traffic-distribution chain.**

**Attribution status: BEHAVIORAL, NOT signature-confirmed.** No IDS/Suricata alerts or YARA/hash matches exist in this evidence set, no internet lookups were performed, and the dropped payload itself was never observed in the clear (it was retrieved over TLS 1.3 with Encrypted Client Hello, which conceals both the SNI and all application data — no key log was provided, so the executable could not be extracted or hashed). The family name above is an assessment based on the following observed TTPs, not a hash/signature match:

- Multi-stage delivery through disposable, recently-registered domains on abuse-favored TLDs (`.sbs`, `.lat`, `.cyou`, `.cc`, `.su`), Cloudflare-fronted for the loader stages.
- A large single-shot binary/archive download (~14.7 MB) from a fake "file hosting" branded domain, arriving ~2.5s after landing on a redirector domain and ~0.5s after a fake download-portal domain — the classic gate → lure → payload pattern of a TDS/ClickFix chain.
- ~21 seconds after the download completes, the host begins beaconing to a new C2 that: (a) harvests a full anti-detect browser fingerprint (Canvas, WebGL renderer/vendor, AudioContext, screen/timezone, installed fonts, plugin list) via a JavaScript payload, POSTs it JSON-encoded to a `/api/set_agent` endpoint, and does this **twice**, self-identifying once as `agent=Chrome` and once as `agent=Edge` from the same host seconds apart — i.e., the malware is impersonating multiple browser identities to the panel rather than being an actual browser session; (b) immediately after, opens 14 back-to-back short-lived TLS connections to the same server and uploads over 2 MB of data in irregular chunks (970B–1.4MB) — the "loot-file-per-POST" exfiltration pattern typical of stealer log uploads (separate files for passwords/cookies/autofill/screenshots/system info).
- A cleartext 404 debug response from the C2 panel leaked its internal file-handling: `cant open archive 172.56.88.98-038485b1855ec7a1ba5bbda042ad17a1.zip`, confirming the panel stores per-victim loot as a ZIP archive named `<external-IP>-<32-char-hex-id>.zip`.
